vii
Decades of remarkable progress against poverty and inequality have given way to a period of
slower and more uneven gains. Between 1990 and 2020, the share of the world’s population
living in extreme poverty fell from 43 percent to 11 percent, driven largely by gains in large
middle-income economies. The number of economies with high inequality, measured by a Gini
index above 40, declined from 70 in 2000 to 42 in 2024. But progress has slowed, and extreme
poverty is increasingly concentrated in a few economies, most of them in Sub-Saharan Africa
and in fragile and conflict-affected situations.
In 2026, an estimated 811 million people, 1 in 10, live below the international extreme poverty
line of $3.00 a day, a rate unchanged since 2019. Without faster growth, the number will rise as
populations grow more quickly where poverty is highest.
Escaping extreme poverty does not guarantee economic security. Nearly half of humanity,
3.7 billion people, live below the $8.30-a-day poverty line typically used to measure poverty in
upper-middle-income countries, leaving many vulnerable to falling back into extreme poverty
after a shock. Weather-related shocks add to this vulnerability: 1.5 billion people, most living
above the extreme poverty line, are exposed to climate hazards but lack the means to cope with
these hazards. At the same time, the growth needed to end extreme poverty in the poorest
countries would add little to global emissions.
This edition has a thematic focus on jobs, which the World Bank Group has made central to its
development agenda toward a world free of poverty on a livable planet. Drawing on new data
for more than 130 economies, it provides the first global profile of the work done by poor and
nonpoor adults.
Jobs are the most direct pathway out of poverty for most households. Poor and nonpoor adults
have similar employment rates. One in three adults in poor households are not employed, many
of whom are women. Poor workers not only earn less, they also support more dependents.
This means that reducing poverty requires both more jobs and better-paying jobs. Expanding
employment can make the greatest difference for households living between the $3.00 and $8.30
poverty lines, while raising the earnings of poor workers can have the greatest impact on the
poorest households.
Foreword

viii
Poverty , ProsPerity , and Planet rePort 2026
How to achieve this differs across countries. Where farms and household enterprises account
for most jobs, raising productivity must go hand in hand with creating opportunities for wage
employment. Where wage employment is established, access to better-paying jobs can lift
households out of poverty. Jobs also help families that have escaped poverty withstand shocks
and avoid falling back and, with this help, build a stronger middle class.
Reducing poverty requires both expanding opportunities to earn a living and increasing the
returns to the work poor people already do. By bringing together new evidence on poverty,
inequality, climate risks, and jobs, this report seeks to help chart a path toward renewed
progress in ending extreme poverty and boosting shared prosperity on a livable planet.
Building on a decade of evidence and analysis, it seeks to help turn this knowledge into
lasting progress.

Co-leads of the report
Kathleen Beegle is a Lead Economist in the Development Research Group at the World
Bank. She co-leads the World Bank Center for Research on Women and Jobs. Her research
focuses on the study of poverty, labor, economic shocks, and methodological studies on
household survey data collection in low-income contexts. She is a regular contributor to the
World Bank’s Development Impact blog. Before returning to the Development Research Group,
she was the Human Development Program Leader for Ghana, Liberia, and Sierra Leone and a
Lead Economist with the Gender Group. Kathleen holds a PhD in economics from Michigan
State University.
Maurizio Bussolo is a Lead Economist in the Distributional Impact of Policies Unit at the
World Bank. He specializes in quantitative analyses of economic policy and development
with research interests spanning both micro- and macroeconomic topics. He led operational
teams in the aftermath of the 2008–09 crisis, negotiating with Latin American and Caribbean
governments on the implementation of reforms to shield the most vulnerable. He previously
worked at the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, the Overseas
Development Institute in London, and Fedesarrollo and Los Andes University in Colombia.
He has extensively published in peer-reviewed journals on trade, growth, poverty, and income
distribution. Maurizio holds a PhD in economics from the University of Warwick.

xv
Ten facts on poverty, prosperity, planet,
and jobs
Poverty
1. The decline in extreme poverty has stalled. In 2026, 811 million people, 1 in 10, are living
on less than $3.00 a day, a rate unchanged since 2019. Had the 2000–13 pace been maintained,
243 million additional people would have escaped poverty. The stagnation is confined to
the extreme line; at $4.20 and $8.30, poverty reduction has kept the earlier pace (refer to
figure 1, panel a).
2. Extreme poverty is concentrated, and demographic patterns will concentrate it further.
More than half the extreme poor are living in nine economies, and, by 2030, 87 percent will
be living in Sub-Saharan Africa, in a fragile and conflict-affected situation, or both (refer to
figure 1, panel b). The population is growing most quickly where poverty rates are the highest;
so, at the 2015–24 pace of economic growth, the global rate and the number of the extreme
poor will be higher in 2030 than today.
3. Escaping extreme poverty has not meant reaching the middle class. Nearly half of humanity,
3.7 billion people, is still living on less than $8.30 a day, the poverty line in upper-middle-
income economies. Most people who have left extreme poverty since 2000 have moved only
into the $3.00–$8.30 band: no longer extremely poor, but not economically secure, and one
shock away from falling back into extreme poverty. The size of the global middle class—people
living on between $8.30 a day and the $28.00 prosperity standard—has roughly doubled as a
share of the world’s population over the same period, but its expansion has been concentrated
in today’s upper-middle-income economies, where the middle class is now the majority.
In lower-middle-income economies, the vulnerable group living on between $3.00 and $8.30 a
day is still the largest, and, in low-income economies, the middle class remains a small minority
(refer to figure 1, panel c).

Prosperity
4. High inequality is retreating across economies but persists across people. The number of
economies with a Gini index above 40 fell from 70 in 2000 to 42 in 2024, and those economies still
above the threshold cut their average Gini from 51 to 46. Nonetheless, one in five people worldwide
is still living in a high-inequality economy, a share unchanged since 2013 (refer to figure 2, panel a),
and 37 economies have never left the above-40 group in 25 years. The concentration of the extreme
poor is happening here, too. The share in high-inequality economies nearly doubled, to 36 percent.
5. The Prosperity Gap halved and then stalled. In 1990, incomes worldwide needed to rise
10.5-fold, on average, to reach the $28.00-a-person-a-day prosperity standard. By 2013, the
Prosperity Gap had fallen to 5.5, and it stood at 4.5 in 2026 (refer to figure 2, panel b, left panel).
Almost all the progress occurred before 2013. Over the latest decade, the gap has narrowed by
only about 1.2 percent a year (refer to figure 2, panel b, right panel). The gap in Sub-Saharan
Africa is at 11.1, twice the global average and roughly where the world stood in 1990.

Planet
6. Climate risk reaches well beyond the poor. Of the 4.6 billion people exposed to a major
climate hazard, 1.5 billion are also highly vulnerable because they lack social protection or access to
basic infrastructure, and most of the highly vulnerable live above the extreme poverty line. The risk
is concentrated in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan and the Sub-Saharan
Africa regions, where nearly half and over a third of the population, respectively, are at high risk,
and almost everyone who is exposed is also vulnerable. In South Asia, by contrast, the share of the
population at risk has been brought below 20 percent by reducing vulnerability (refer to figure 3,
panel a). Globally, the share of people at high risk fell from one in three in 2010 to one in six in 2024,
although the number of people exposed rose by about 550 million.

xix
main messa Ges
7. Emissions are still rising, but not where the poor are. Global greenhouse gas emissions,
excluding those from land use, land use change, and forestry, reached 52.8 metric gigatons of

9. More jobs and better-paying jobs both reduce poverty, but they reach different people.
Raising employment in poor households to 75 percent, the rate poor men already attain, cuts
extreme poverty by a fifth; raising education to the nonpoor average cuts extreme poverty by
nearly half; and switching poor workers into nonagricultural employment or into wage work
cuts it by a quarter to a third. All these simulations reduce the depth of poverty as well (refer to
figure 4, panel c). The gains from better pay accrue mainly to the poorest. The gains from more
work accrue mainly to the near-poor, among whom the nonworking adults are mostly women.
10. Poverty falls as the work of the poor becomes more productive, and, in the poorest
economies, the work is mostly on farms and in household enterprises, not in wage jobs. In
richer economies, households that move into wage employment are much more likely to escape
poverty, while those that move into self-employment are not. In the poorest economies, the
gain from wage employment is about a third as large, and the gain from self-employment, on
the farm or off the farm, is not far below (refer to figure 4, panel d). The lowest rung of the
ladder out of poverty is work on the farm, where higher yields raise earnings. Each step up
represents a higher-productivity activity. The reach of the ladder is limited only by the ability of
firms on the upper rungs to create jobs. So far, in the poorest countries, most of the movement
upward has ended in microenterprise or self-employment activities rather than higher-earning
wage jobs. Jobs matter in a second way as well: They keep households from falling back into
poverty. It is this protection that transforms the exits from extreme poverty into a growing
middle class.

1
The reduction in global poverty over the past generation ranks among the great global
achievements of economic development in the postwar era. In 1990, 43 percent of the world’s
population was living in extreme poverty. By 2020, the share was about 11 percent, and,
now, more than two-thirds of humanity is living in economies in which extreme poverty has
effectively ended, up from a fifth in 2000. This achievement is the standard against which
the present situation must be measured, and the present falls short. Progress against extreme
poverty has come to a standstill. After rising during the COVID pandemic and then recovering,
the extreme poverty rate has remained essentially unchanged. In 2026, an estimated 811 million
people—one person in 10—were living below the international poverty line of $3.00 a day.
The slowdown predates the pandemic and has persisted since. Had poverty continued to fall at
the 2000–13 pace, roughly 240 million fewer people would be poor today.
The picture is different at higher poverty lines. At $4.20 and $8.30 a day (the standards typical
of lower-middle- and upper-middle-income economies), poverty reduction has broadly
maintained the earlier pace. Even so, nearly half of humanity—3.7 billion people—are still
living on less than $8.30 a day. The share has fallen modestly, but population growth has offset
much of the gain, keeping the absolute number stubbornly high.
Many people who have escaped extreme poverty are also living only slightly above the
$3.00 line and are therefore vulnerable to falling back after a major economic or climate
shock. El Niño illustrates this risk in real time. Still intensifying toward a projected peak in
late 2026 and already approaching record levels in the modern period, it is already driving
emerging impacts on food security, incomes, and livelihoods across the globe, with effects
on nutrition and human capital that could persist for years. The conflict in the Middle East
is a second source of pressure, raising energy prices and, with them, the cost of fertilizer and
of transporting food. Before the conflict, extreme poverty in 2026 was projected to affect
808 million people rather than the 811 million people now estimated (refer to box 1.2).
With a global median income of $9.20 a day, most of the world’s population is living below or
only slightly above the $8.30 line. The world’s middle class—the population between this line
and the prosperity standard of $28.00 a day—remains a minority of humanity (refer to box 1.3).
It has roughly doubled as a share of the world’s population since 2000, with almost all of the

expansion in middle-income economies, but the group that has escaped extreme poverty
without reaching security has remained close to a third of humanity throughout. Without a
change in the trajectory of poverty reduction, the 2020s will close as the first decade in more
than a generation without meaningful progress against extreme poverty.
Read together, the findings of this report form a single argument, summarized as 9 facts in the
main messages section and developed in the sections that follow. On poverty, the stagnation
at the extreme line is compounded by concentration: The extreme poor live increasingly in a
small group of economies, in Sub-Saharan Africa, and in fragile and conflict-affected situations,
where populations are growing most quickly, so the global poverty rate will rise even as most
national rates edge down. On prosperity, most people who have escaped extreme poverty
have not reached the middle class, and nearly half of humanity is still living on less than $8.30
a day and remain vulnerable to falling back. Fewer economies are now highly unequal, but
the share of the world’s people living in these economies has not fallen, and the closing of the
Global Prosperity Gap has slowed to a fraction of the earlier pace. On the planet, climate risk
is reaching people far above the poverty line: while emissions are growing in economies where
the poor do not live, ending extreme poverty would add little to global emissions. On jobs, the
poor rely almost entirely on their labor; work nearly as much as the nonpoor, but earn less per
household member; and their employment has been eroding. More jobs and better-paying jobs
both reduce poverty, but the gains from better pay accrue mainly to the extreme poor, and the
gains from more work accrue mainly to the near-poor. In the poorest economies, the route out
of poverty runs through leaving low-return agriculture rather more than through wage work.
In poorer and richer economies alike, the source of the exit is productivity growth on farms,
where higher yields allow workers to move into nonfarm work, and in firms, which expand and
hire wage workers.
Tracking the global path to ending
extreme poverty, with jobs at the center
The Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report tracks the progress in the effort to reduce extreme
poverty and boost shared prosperity on a livable planet through eight vision indicators: the
global poverty rates at the $3.00- and $8.30-a-person-a-day poverty lines, the Global Prosperity
Gap, the count of high-inequality economies, and five planetary indicators—greenhouse gas
emissions, people at high risk from climate hazards, the health of key ecosystems, food and
nutrition insecurity, and access to water and sanitation—that track the natural conditions on
which well-being depends. In the spirit of the earlier reports, this edition has a thematic focus:
jobs and their role in poverty reduction.1
Most of the eight indicators change slowly year-on-year. Each edition of the report strives
to dig more deeply than the often slowly changing headline statistics. This edition confirms
well-established findings on education and access to better jobs, the vulnerability of children,

3
overvie W
the persistence of inequality, the exposure to climate risk, the difficulty of creating better jobs
in rural areas, and the concentration of poor workers in subsistence agriculture and nonfarm
self-employment. At the same time, this report has three new elements worth highlighting. First,
it presents new data. The coverage of household surveys has been expanded in regions that
earlier survey editions could not observe; the five planetary indicators are included for the first
time; and a global database merging labor market indicators and poverty status—a combination
no earlier collection provided—has been assembled to unpack the links between poverty and
jobs. Second, this report offers new analysis: decompositions that separate progress within
countries from the changing composition of the world; duration analysis of inequality;
subnational trajectories and household typologies; the first global jobs profile of the poor
based on a comparison of working hours by poverty status; panel survey evidence on labor
transitions; and counterfactual simulations that assess the employment and earnings barriers
the poor face. Third, it offers new findings, including that poor workers average fewer rather
than more weekly hours on the job relative to nonpoor workers and that shifts into wage
employment yield less poverty reduction in low-income economies than in richer economies.
This report opens with a sobering projection. If economies grow over the coming years at the
per capita economic growth rates experienced from 2015 to 2024, both the global extreme
poverty rate and the number of people living in extreme poverty will be higher in 2030 than
today. This would not represent a mere pause, but a stunning reversal of the improvement in
well-being of the preceding decades. Only sustained annual global economic growth of around
4 percent per capita would bring the global extreme poverty rate down to near the 3 percent
target by 2050. However, this rate would be double the average country growth rate observed
over the past 25 years.
The mechanism behind the projected reversal is linked to demographic trends (specifically
population growth) and insufficient economic growth. Poverty rates in most high-poverty
economies are projected to decline, though only marginally. The weight of these economies as
a share of the world’s population is expected to rise. The population is growing most quickly
precisely in the locations that exhibit the highest poverty rates and that also often face conflict,
fragility, and climate vulnerability. Thus, the global extreme poverty rate would be pulled
upward even as the extreme poverty rates in most economies would hold steady or improve.
The distinction matters for policy: The challenge is not a diffuse global failure of development,
but the clustering of clear needs in an identifiable group of economies.
Concentration is a key fact of global
extreme poverty and inequality
Concentration recurs across the findings of this report. More than half the world’s extreme
poor live in only 9 economies, while three-quarters live in 20 economies. Global poverty is
concentrated both from a regional perspective and in terms of fragility. By 2030, 87 percent of

4
Poverty , ProsPerity , and Planet rePort 2026
the world’s extreme poor will be living in Sub-Saharan Africa or in fragile and conflict-affected
states in Sub-Saharan Africa or elsewhere.
The places where extreme poverty persists are also increasingly places characterized by high
inequality. One in five people in the world are living in economies classified as highly unequal.
Among the world’s extreme poor, the share is two in five, and this share has nearly doubled
since 2000. The overlap compounds the challenge because high inequality weakens the poverty-
reducing power of growth: The same rate of economic growth produces less poverty reduction
in highly unequal economies.
The report’s count of high-inequality economies illustrates what a headline figure may conceal.
The count fell from 70 in 2000 to 42 in 2024, a decline of more than one-third. Underlying this
trend, the report’s fresh duration analysis reveals two findings that emphasize the stubborn
persistence of inequality. In 2000–24, the Gini index never rose above 40 in 79 economies and
never fell below 40 in 37 economies. The middle is thin. Few economies spent between 5 and
20 years above the threshold before falling below the threshold. High inequality is apparently
not a transitory state through which economies pass. It is a chronic condition either avoided or
endured for decades. The fall in the count of high-inequality economies should thus not be read
as evidence that escape from high-inequality status is easy.
More encouraging is the fact that, among the 37 economies in which high inequality has
endured, the average Gini index has declined from about 51 to about 46, and the decline has
been broad across the distribution. Roughly a quarter of these economies now stand within
three points of the threshold of 40. Transitions from high to moderate inequality are rare, but
the progress that precedes an exit from high inequality accumulates across years before it is
registered in a headline figure. Read together, these two findings demonstrate that it is more
difficult to exit a situation of high inequality than the falling count suggests and that more
exiting is under way than the count reveals.
The report’s second prosperity indicator corroborates the diagnosis reached through the
poverty data. The Global Prosperity Gap—the average factor by which incomes must be
multiplied to reach a dignified and secure daily standard of living—has narrowed by half
since 1990, but the narrowing in the gap has slowed appreciably since 2013. Of note, the
countries in the East Asia and Pacific region have achieved remarkable improvements
toward closing the gap by a 4.4 percent reduction per year. China accounts for much of the
progress. In Sub-Saharan Africa, consistent with the stalling poverty reduction, the pace is
0.7 percent a year. The region’s three most populous economies, the Democratic Republic
of Congo, Ethiopia, and Nigeria, account for 40 percent of the regional Prosperity Gap. All
three are currently classified as fragile and conflict-affected states. Larger populations are
only part of the story. Nigeria accounts for 18 percent of the population and 16 percent of the
gap, and Ethiopia, for 10 percent and 8 percent, respectively. Y et, the Democratic Republic
of Congo makes up 9 percent of the region’s population, but accounts for 16 percent of its
Prosperity Gap.

Deprivations extend beyond monetary
measures: A deteriorating planet
threatens the gains against poverty
Measured across 103 economies, 17 percent of people are multidimensionally poor, that is,
they are deprived in at least one of three dimensions (monetary welfare, education, and access
to basic infrastructure), while 11 percent are deprived according to the monetary welfare
dimension alone. This difference between multidimensional and monetary poverty is widest
in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, where it is driven by deprivations in education and
sanitation.
The five planetary indicators tracked in this report reveal a further source of vulnerability.
On balance, the situation is deteriorating: Greenhouse gas emissions are at record levels;
ecosystems are shrinking; and food insecurity remains above prepandemic levels in many
regions. Access to water and sanitation has improved steadily, and the share of people at
high risk from climate hazards has fallen even as the absolute number of people facing such
risk has grown. But progress is uneven; the gaps that remain are vast; and the pressures are
affecting disproportionately the poor and those people who have only recently climbed out
of poverty, thereby eroding the foundations on which durable poverty reduction depends.
Climate risk is an important direct channel through which a deteriorating planet impacts
poor households. The report’s climate risk indicator combines exposure to damaging
climate hazards—such as flooding, drought, tropical cyclones, or extreme heat expected
over a lifetime—with vulnerability, that is, a lack of capacity to cope if a hazard strikes. The
vulnerability can be physical (limited access to water and electricity or limited mobility) or
economic (low income, little education, no social protection, no access to financial services).
Around 4.6 billion people live in exposed areas, and 2.7 billion live in highly vulnerable
conditions; about 1.5 billion people experience both types of vulnerability. The drivers of
multidimensional poverty also drive climate vulnerability. The same lack of schooling and
missing infrastructure that identify a household as multidimensionally poor can convert a flood
or a drought from a hazard into a catastrophe.
Globally, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions continue to increase year on year. GHG emissions,
excluding those from land use, forestry, and changes in land use, reached 52.8 metric gigatons of
carbon dioxide equivalent (GtCO₂e) in 2024, about 48.0 percent above the levels in 2000,
although they rose by only 0.6 percent in 2024. While the rate of increase seems to be
declining since 2000, emissions have yet to peak and decline. This will lead to continued global
temperature increases and global impacts, including increased damages from weather events,
rising costs of adaptation, and exposure of more people to risks they may not be able to absorb.
Emissions per unit of gross domestic product are nonetheless declining. Almost all major
emitters have reduced emissions intensity in recent years, and several of the largest emitters

6
Poverty , ProsPerity , and Planet rePort 2026
(Japan, the United States, and several European Union countries) have been reducing the level
of absolute emissions over the past decade.
The health of key ecosystems is also deteriorating. Tropical primary forest loss reached
6.7 million hectares in 2024, nearly twice the level of 2023. Fires overtook agriculture as
the leading driver of loss. Forests, wetlands, and other ecosystems support livelihoods and
economic activity by regulating water, sustaining agricultural production, storing carbon,
and reducing exposure to environmental hazards. These services are especially important in
poorer economies, where renewable natural capital represents a large share of national wealth.
If ecosystems are degraded, poor households lose resources and forms of protection that are
difficult to replace.
Food and nutrition insecurity remain widespread. In 2024, 2.3 billion people experienced
moderate or severe food insecurity, while around 150 million children under 5 years of age
were stunted, which is associated with consequences that can persist throughout life. Climate
shocks, ecosystem degradation, and food price volatility can deepen these deprivations,
especially among households that spend a large share of their incomes on food and have few
assets available to cope.
Progress on water and sanitation is also too slow. Around 2.1 billion people still lack access to
safely managed drinking water. Rural populations and people in Sub-Saharan Africa face the
largest gaps. These deficits are a form of deprivation, and they also raise the vulnerability to
climate shocks. Droughts, floods, and extreme heat place the greatest strain on communities
where water and sanitation systems are already weak.
The planetary indicators contradict the widely held presumption that there is a conflict
between the goal of ending extreme poverty and the goal of protecting the climate. The effort
to eradicate extreme poverty is estimated to add less than 5 percent to global emissions. The
extreme poor contribute the least to global emissions, but are the most vulnerable to the
consequences of climate change. A benefit-cost comparison makes the asymmetry explicit.
Weighing the people whom a percentage point of economic growth lifts out of poverty on a
scale against the people who may be pushed into poverty by the emissions associated with
the economic growth yields a benefit-cost ratio above 100 in the poorest countries and a
corresponding ratio below 1 in many of the richest countries. Economic growth in places
where the poor are concentrated has poverty reduction benefits that dwarf the near-term costs
of the associated emissions.
More and better jobs are needed to tackle
global poverty
Poor households have—almost without exception—only a single productive asset: human
capital. Land, physical capital, and savings are scarce at the bottom of the distribution, and the
routes to acquiring these assets are limited. Since it was initiated in 2016, this report series has

7
overvie W
recorded the traits in the global profile of the poor, such as rural residence, low educational
attainment, and the high share of children in the household, but has not detailed the link
to jobs. This shortcoming has been caused by the lack of a sufficient database combining
information on poverty and information on jobs at a global scale. This report has relied on the
construction of such a database, which covers 96 percent of the world’s population. The jobs
profile complements the familiar profile of the traits of poverty.
Rural poverty is associated with agricultural work. Two-thirds of extremely poor workers are
in farm jobs and are among the most exposed to climate variability and ecosystem stress. The
education deficit becomes an earnings deficit among these workers. Poor workers earn little
because the skills and knowledge they have are poorly matched to the demands of higher-
paying labor markets. The demographic profile illustrates a dependency burden. A working
adult in a poor household supports roughly three times as many dependents as a working adult
in a rich household. The missing second earner in poor households is most often a woman.
Employment among women is lowest globally among households in the lower middle of the
distribution. Low female labor market participation is a structural driver of household poverty.
Labor income is the product of two factors: the amount of work a household supplies and the
amount of earnings people receive if they work. This report examines poverty through each of
these factors. It finds that neither factor alone accounts for the persistence of poverty and that
addressing only one of these factors is insufficient to end poverty.
On employment rates, the poor fall only slightly short of the nonpoor. About three in five
working-age adults in poor households are employed, some 6 percentage points below the rate
among adults in nonpoor households. Joblessness thus accounts for only part of global poverty.
The near parity in employment rates is a global average. The employment gap between the poor
and the nonpoor is small or absent in poorer economies and wide in richer economies. It also
conceals two shortfalls. Poor workers put in about three to four fewer hours a week relative to
nonpoor workers, whether wage earners or self-employed, and the gap is largest in the poorest
countries and among the self-employed. So, more work means not only a job but sufficient
hours in the job. In poor households, the shortfall in employment is concentrated among
women. Men are employed at rates of about 75 percent; women at far lower rates.
Over the past two decades, the gap between the poor and the nonpoor has widened. From
2003 to 2024, employment rates among the poor fell in 88 of 138 countries, and, in 99 of 137
countries, they grew more slowly or fell more quickly than the rates among the nonpoor at the
$8.30-a-person-a-day poverty line (in 2021 purchasing power parity terms). Longer schooling
among the young does not account for the decline, which is present among adults ages 25–64 as
well. This report points to three mechanisms that it does not test directly. First, agriculture has
shed workers more quickly than other sectors have absorbed them, and the poor, concentrated
in agriculture, have been the first to be affected. Second, technical change may have lowered the
demand for less well educated workers. Third, women leaving agriculture face constraints in
taking up other work, ranging from care responsibilities and social norms to transport. Among
the poor, the exit from farming may more often therefore end in nonemployment.

8
Poverty , ProsPerity , and Planet rePort 2026
Combining both employment rates and earnings, this report shows that, over these two
decades, growth in earnings per worker accounted for essentially all the welfare growth
among the poorest households, while declines in employment rates reduced welfare
growth. Poverty continued to decline as long as the growth in earnings more than offset
the shrinking employment rate among the poor. The past two decades thus represent a
missed opportunity rather than a verdict on employment. Had the level of employment
among the poor been maintained, the same earnings growth would have reduced poverty
more quickly.
How much can more jobs and better-paying jobs contribute to poverty reduction? Simulations
undertaken for this report show that raising the employment rate among poor households to
a benchmark of 75 percent of working-age adults would reduce the global poverty rate by a
fifth. This is roughly the employment rate already observed among men in poor households,
among poor households two decades ago, and in the richest quintile of the global population.
Reaching this rate would therefore require closing much of the gender gap in employment
because nearly all the shortfall is among women. Raising the earnings associated with the jobs
held by the poor would reduce poverty further. Lifting the educational attainment of poor
workers to the nonpoor average would cut the extreme poverty rate by nearly half. Labor
movements out of agriculture and out of self-employment into wage work would contribute
additional rate reductions.
In these simulations, the additional employment and the higher earnings reach different
populations. The earnings gains are proportionally greatest among the poorest. The
simulations assign broadly similar absolute gains to workers with similar characteristics,
and, so, the gain is proportionally largest among the poorest workers. Meanwhile, the
employment gains are concentrated among the near-poor, among whom the nonworking
adults are disproportionately women. Better pay or higher returns to work (such as among
smallholders or microenterprises) benefits the destitute the most. More work benefits the
near-poor the most.
Better-paying work depends on
productivity growth and the jobs that
firms create
The simulations reported above draw on household surveys, which describe the labor market
from the viewpoint of households. The employment and earnings the surveys record represent
the joint product of the labor that households supply and the demand for this labor. Household
surveys provide information on workers and their families, but only limited information on the
firms that might employ these people or on the smallholder and microenterprise ecosystems

9
overvie W
in which the self-employed work. The simulations also hold wages fixed and displace no
incumbents. So, the impacts they report represent upper bounds.
What has happened over the past two decades shows why these limits matter. The contraction
of subsistence farming has fed mostly into nonagricultural forms of microenterprise or self-
employment, mostly in services, rather than into higher-paying wage work. This represents a
pattern of incomplete structural transformation. The distinction matters because a given rate
of growth reduces poverty more quickly if it is accompanied by a movement of workers and
earnings out of low-return agriculture than if the sectoral composition of the movement is
neutral. Whether the poor can reach better-paying work depends on two factors: whether such
work is created and whether workers have the skills and qualifications employers in higher-
paying work require. Raising the productivity of the work the poor already do, especially on
smallholder farms, is a route that does not depend on the creation of such jobs, and it is the
route with the shortest horizon.
The simulations are not the only evidence. Additional evidence is supplied by household
surveys that track job transitions into wage jobs and self-employment, out of farming, or into or
out of work altogether and that track whether households escaped poverty or fell into poverty
during the same years. Longitudinal surveys in 41 economies confirm that both more work and
better-paying work are associated with poverty reduction. However, the job transitions that
drive this result vary. A transition into a wage job is associated with poverty reduction in richer
economies, while a transition out of agriculture into nonagricultural work of any kind matters
most in poorer economies. If the share of a poor household’s working-age members in wage
employment rises by 10 percentage points, the household’s chance of escaping poverty increases
by 2.4 percentage points in upper-middle-income economies and by 2.2 percentage points in
high-income economies, but by only 0.8 percentage points in low- and lower-middle-income
economies. A shift into nonwage work raises the chance of escaping poverty by 0.5 percentage
points in the poorest economies, not far below the corresponding effect of wage employment
in these same economies, while the estimate is not distinguishable from zero in upper-middle-
income economies and negative in high-income economies. Poor households in the poorest
economies are held back twice over. The wage work within their reach may not generate the
income necessary to lift these households out of poverty, as these estimates show, and such
work is also scarce. Over the period under observation, the share of working-age adults in wage
employment rose by 3.4 percentage points among poor households in the poorest economies,
against 7.7 percentage points in high-income economies. Access to a job and access to decent
pay are both needed, and, in the poorest economies, both are in short supply.
The longitudinal data also show that, in addition to lifting households out of poverty,
employment helps keep households from sliding into poverty, though not always through the
same type of work. Self-employment in agriculture and outside agriculture protects households
against falling into poverty in rich and poor economies alike.

Poverty , ProsPerity , and Planet rePort 2026
Concentrated poverty can be tackled, but
progress is unlikely to be swift
The findings of this report support neither complacency nor despair. Most of the world has left
extreme poverty behind, and the poverty that remains is concentrated geographically, socially,
and across the dimensions of deprivation. Concentration establishes where the remaining
poverty is located and who suffers from this poverty. Designing policies to reduce poverty
depends on understanding both dimensions. The task will not be easy. This report documents
that poverty is concentrated among the countries and the households that have been the
hardest to reach; in fragile states; in regions vulnerable to climate risks; and in families with low
education, low skills, and many dependents.
The challenge of concentrated poverty cannot be separated from the condition of the planet
on which the poor live. The coming decades will bring continued warming, mounting pressure
on ecosystems, and growing food and water stress. At the same time, poverty reduction must
accelerate. Investments in climate resilience can therefore also be investments in poverty
reduction. Protecting ecosystems helps preserve the natural asset base on which many poor
households depend. Limiting the peaks and duration of warming reduces the risks borne
disproportionately by people who have contributed the least to the problem and possess the
fewest resources to cope.
Each route out of poverty examined above—employment restored to a level the poor attained
two decades ago, schooling raised to the level the nonpoor already have, shifts into better-
paying jobs, and the economic growth needed for all three—can be quantified: how much
poverty each would remove and which poor households each would reach. Such change rarely
occurs quickly. Education among the poor typically yields impacts only after the poor cohorts
successfully complete the transition from school to work. The barriers are great. Employment
rates among the poor, especially poor women, are stagnant or falling. In some regions, a sizable
share of the population remains vulnerable to climate hazards. Inequality is often persistent.
Still, progress is possible even under such challenging circumstances, as demonstrated by the
improvements in well-being over the last three decades. The broad focus of this report, to
monitor this progress, is not meant to be a passive record of slowly moving numbers, but a road
map that keeps the conditions and the opportunities for poverty reduction in view.

Poverty and Shared Prosperity Reports 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2022.

Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report 2026: Jobs at the Center of Poverty Eradication
assesses global progress toward ending extreme poverty and boosting shared prosperity
on a livable planet. After three decades of historic gains, extreme poverty reduction has
stalled. In 2026, an estimated 811 million people, 1 in 10 worldwide, are living on less than
$3.00 a day, while nearly half of humanity is living on less than $8.30 a day. Poverty is
increasingly concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa and fragile and conflict-affected situations,
where rapid population growth, insufficient economic growth, and exposure to various
shocks make progress extremely difficult.
Through the deeply probing lens of poverty, prosperity, and planetary sustainability, the
report finds that the number of economies with high inequality is falling. Yet, many people,
including a growing share of the extreme poor, are still living in highly unequal economies.
And progress in closing the Global Prosperity Gap—an indicator that combines the tracking
of both progress in average income and improvements in equity—has also slowed. Climate
hazards, ecosystem degradation, food insecurity, and inadequate water and sanitation are
threatening the gains in development, especially among those people and households with
the fewest resources to withstand and recover from shocks. Ending extreme poverty would
add relatively little to the cost or impacts of global emissions, demonstrating that poverty
reduction and climate protection are not competing goals.
Placing jobs at the center, the report offers new evidence on how employment and earnings
shape household welfare. Using survey data linking poverty with labor market outcomes, it
offers a global profile of poor and nonpoor workers and examines pathways out of poverty
through job opportunities. Poor people work nearly as much as the nonpoor but earn less,
work fewer hours, and support more dependents. And one in three poor people have no
employment. Both more jobs and better-paying jobs will reduce poverty, but the effects of
each reach different groups. Increasing earnings matters most for the poorest, while increasing
rates of employment, particularly among women, benefits the near-poor the most.
Poverty reduction requires that access to income-generating opportunities expands and
that the returns to the work poor people already perform increase. This report—by tracking
where poverty is concentrated, the progress on inequality, and the status of measures of
a livable planet, combined with a unique profile of the work of the poor—seeks to inspire a
data-driven agenda for reinvigorating global progress in these many dimensions.
